claim: 5′-terminal modifications, including triethylene glycol (TEG) moieties, consistently increase the frequency of precision editing in the germlines of C. elegans, zebrafish, and mice, and in cultured human cells.
source: Here, we explore chemical modifications to both double-stranded and single-stranded DNA-repair templates. We describe 5′-terminal modifications, including in its simplest form the incorporation of triethylene glycol (TEG) moieties, that consistently increase the frequency of precision editing in the germlines of three animal models (Caenorhabditis elegans, zebrafish, mice) and in cultured human cells.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the main finding that 5′-terminal modifications increase precision editing frequency across multiple model systems, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: RNA::TEG-modified donors increased HDR frequency to a maximum of 52% GFP+ cells at 1.2 pmol, compared to 25% for unmodified donors at 1.6 pmol in HEK293T TLR cells.
source: Strikingly, the frequency of HDR increased with the amount of RNA::TEG-modified donor to a maximal 52% GFP+ cells at 1.2 pmol of donor before falling off at higher amounts of donor (Figure 1B). By contrast, a maximum HDR frequency of only 25% GFP+ cells was observed at 1.6 pmol of unmodified donor.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the TLR assay shown in Figure 1B, with specific quantitative measurements provided.

claim: RNA::TEG-modified donors are approximately 4-fold more potent than unmodified donors in HEK293T cells.
source: Notably, 0.4 pmol RNA::TEG-modified donor was as efficient as 1.6 pmol unmodified donor, suggesting that the modified donor is ~4-fold more potent than the unmodified donor (Figure 1B).
evidence: The potency comparison is based on dose-response data from the TLR assay, comparing the amounts of modified vs. unmodified donors needed to achieve similar HDR efficiency.

claim: PNA oligos linked to nuclear localization signal peptide did not enhance HDR when annealed to RNA::TEG-modified donors.
source: Annealing these PNA oligos was well tolerated and did not diminish HDR, however neither did they enhance HDR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-D comparing HDR efficiency with and without PNA::NLS.

claim: 2′OMe-RNA, TEG, or covalent RNA::TEG moieties at 1.2 pmol all boosted HDR while reducing NHEJ events in the TLR assay.
source: Nucleofection of 1.2 pmol donors modified with 2′OMe-RNA, TEG, or covalent RNA::TEG moieties all boosted HDR while reducing NHEJ events (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the TLR assay shown in Figure 1D and E, measuring both HDR (GFP+) and NHEJ (mCherry+) outcomes.

claim: Increasing the length of the ethylene glycol moiety (3, 6, or 12 repeats) supported similar levels of HDR with or without the 2′OMe-RNA moiety.
source: Increasing the length of the ethylene glycol moiety (3, 6, or 12 repeats) supported similar levels of HDR with or without the 2′OMe-RNA moiety (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F comparing HDR efficiency across different ethylene glycol lengths.

claim: Donors with TEG modification at both 5′-ends yielded slightly better HDR efficiencies than donors with modification at only one of the two 5′-ends.
source: Finally, donors with TEG modification at both 5′-ends yielded slightly better HDR efficiencies than donors with modification at only one of the two 5′-ends (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G comparing single-end vs. double-end TEG modifications.

claim: Donors with RNA::TEG modification at both 5′-ends or at only one of the 5′-ends yielded similar HDR efficiencies.
source: However, donors with RNA::TEG modification at both 5′-ends or at only one of the 5′-ends yielded similar HDR efficiencies (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G comparing single-end vs. double-end RNA::TEG modifications.

claim: TEG or RNA::TEG donors increased HDR levels at the TOMM20 locus in HEK293T cells by 2-fold compared to unmodified dsDNA donor.
source: We found that TEG or RNA::TEG donors consistently exhibited increased HDR levels in HEK293T cells as measured by the fraction of cells expressing eGFP at TOMM20 (2-fold), at GAPDH (3-fold), and at SEC61B (5-fold) when compared to unmodified dsDNA donor (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from eGFP integration assays at endogenous loci, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TEG or RNA::TEG donors increased HDR levels at the GAPDH locus in HEK293T cells by 3-fold compared to unmodified dsDNA donor.
source: We found that TEG or RNA::TEG donors consistently exhibited increased HDR levels in HEK293T cells as measured by the fraction of cells expressing eGFP at TOMM20 (2-fold), at GAPDH (3-fold), and at SEC61B (5-fold) when compared to unmodified dsDNA donor (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from eGFP integration assays at endogenous loci, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TEG or RNA::TEG donors increased HDR levels at the SEC61B locus in HEK293T cells by 5-fold compared to unmodified dsDNA donor.
source: We found that TEG or RNA::TEG donors consistently exhibited increased HDR levels in HEK293T cells as measured by the fraction of cells expressing eGFP at TOMM20 (2-fold), at GAPDH (3-fold), and at SEC61B (5-fold) when compared to unmodified dsDNA donor (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from eGFP integration assays at endogenous loci, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: RNA::TEG-modified donors increased HDR at the TOMM20 locus in human foreskin fibroblasts (HFF) cells by 2.3-fold.
source: RNA::TEG-modified donors also substantially increased HDR in two cell types that are less amenable to editing, increasing HDR at the TOMM20 locus in human foreskin fibroblasts (HFF) cells (2.3-fold) and at the Gapdh locus in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells (6-fold) (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from eGFP integration assays in HFF cells, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: RNA::TEG-modified donors increased HDR at the Gapdh locus in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells by 6-fold.
source: RNA::TEG-modified donors also substantially increased HDR in two cell types that are less amenable to editing, increasing HDR at the TOMM20 locus in human foreskin fibroblasts (HFF) cells (2.3-fold) and at the Gapdh locus in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells (6-fold) (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from eGFP integration assays in CHO cells, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: At 1.2 and 2.4 pmol, RNA::TEG-modified donors yielded 2-fold more precise edits at the EMX1 locus compared to unmodified donors in HEK293T cells.
source: At 1.2 and 2.4 pmol, RNA::TEG-modified donors yielded 2-fold more precise edits compared to the unmodified donors.
evidence: The claim is supported by deep sequencing data quantifying precise editing outcomes at the EMX1 locus.

claim: At 5 pmol donor concentration, the gap in efficacy between unmodified and RNA::TEG-modified donors narrowed to 16% (72.8% vs. 89.5%) precise reads at the EMX1 locus.
source: When even higher doses (5 pmol) were used, the gap in efficacy between unmodified and RNA::TEG-modified donors narrowed to just 16% ( 72.8% vs. 89.5%) precise reads (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2H, demonstrating dose-dependent effects.

claim: TEG-modified donors exhibited no benefit over unmodified donors at the EMX1 locus in HEK293T cells.
source: In this assay, donors modified with TEG alone exhibited no benefit over unmodified donors (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA::TEG modification at the 5′-end of a long (800 nt) ssDNA donor significantly boosted HDR compared to unmodified ssDNA donor in the TLR assay.
source: Using the TLR assay, we found that addition of RNA::TEG at the 5′-end of a long (800 nt) ssDNA donor significantly boosted HDR compared to the unmodified ssDNA donor.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the TLR assay using long ssDNA donors.

claim: The RNA::TEG-modified 800 nt ssDNA donor reached maximal HDR (22.5% GFP(+) cells) at 6–8 pmol donor amounts.
source: The frequency of HDR increased with the dose of ssDNA donor, reaching maximal HDR (22.5% GFP(+)cells) at 6–8 pmol donor amounts (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The RNA::TEG-modified 800 nt ssDNA donor was greater than 4-fold more potent than the unmodified donor, reaching 16% GFP(+) cells at ~2 pmol whereas the unmodified donor required 8 pmol.
source: The RNA::TEG-modified donor was greater than 4-fold more potent than the unmodified donor reaching a threshold of 16% GFP(+) cells at a concentration of ∼2 pmol whereas achieving the same threshold of 16% required 8 pmol of unmodified donor (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3A, comparing potency of modified vs. unmodified donors.

claim: RNA::TEG and unmodified 66 nt ssODN donors produced similar maximal levels of HDR (47.5–52.8% BFP(+) cells) in K562 cells.
source: Using 66 nt long ssODN donors and titrating the amount over a range of 0.01–40 pmol, we found that RNA::TEG and unmodified donors produced similar maximal levels of HDR (47.5–52.8% BFP(+) cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data from the GFP-to-BFP conversion assay in K562 cells.

claim: Maximal HDR with 66 nt ssODN donors required 10-fold less RNA::TEG-modified ssODN than unmodified donors in K562 cells.
source: However, maximal HDR required 10-fold less RNA::TEG-modified ssODN than unmodified donors (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3B, demonstrating increased potency of modified donors.

claim: 2′OMe-RNA, RNA::TEG, or TEG moieties at the 3′-terminus did not enhance HDR compared to unmodified ssODN.
source: Interestingly, 2′OMe-RNA, RNA::TEG, or TEG moieties at the 3′-terminus did not enhance HDR compared to unmodified ssODN, and moreover, they blocked the ability of 2′OMe-RNA, RNA::TEG, or TEG moieties at the 5′-end to enhance HDR (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, testing various modification positions.

claim: 3′-terminal modifications with 2′OMe-RNA, RNA::TEG, or TEG blocked the ability of 5′-end modifications to enhance HDR.
source: Interestingly, 2′OMe-RNA, RNA::TEG, or TEG moieties at the 3′-terminus did not enhance HDR compared to unmodified ssODN, and moreover, they blocked the ability of 2′OMe-RNA, RNA::TEG, or TEG moieties at the 5′-end to enhance HDR (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, demonstrating antagonistic effects of 3′ modifications.

claim: HDR was neither enhanced nor impeded by phosphorothioate (PS) linkages placed at 5′- or 3′-terminal linkages at the doses tested.
source: By contrast, HDR was neither enhanced nor impeded by phosphorothioate (PS) linkages placed at 5′- or 3′-terminal linkages at the doses tested (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, testing PS modifications.

claim: The mechanism of HDR improvement by 5′-modifications requires an available 3′-OH.
source: Taken together these findings suggest that the mechanism of HDR improvement requires an available 3′-OH.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that 3′-terminal modifications block HDR enhancement, suggesting the 3′-OH is necessary for the mechanism.

claim: TEG- and RNA::TEG-modified donors produced about twice as many GFP(+) progeny per injected C. elegans animal than unmodified donors at the csr-1 locus.
source: The TEG- and RNA::TEG-modified donors produced about twice as many GFP(+) progeny per injected animal than did the unmodified donor (Figure 4B and E, two representative broods per donor).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from C. elegans germline editing shown in Figure 4B and E.

claim: Among Roller progeny in C. elegans, end-modified donors increased the fraction of GFP(+) Roller progeny by several fold at the eft-3 locus.
source: Among the Roller cohort, which was previously shown to exhibit lower editing efficiency (Ghanta and Mello, 2020), end-modified donors increased the fraction of GFP(+) Roller progeny by several fold.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from C. elegans germline editing, with citation to previous work establishing the Roller cohort context.

claim: Unmodified eft-3 donor produced 12.6% GFP-positive Rollers, while TEG- and RNA::TEG-modified eft-3 donors produced 57.1% and 49% GFP-positive Rollers, respectively.
source: For example, whereas the unmodified eft-3 donor produced only 12.6% GFP-positive Rollers, the TEG- and RNA::TEG-modified eft-3 donors produced 57.1% and 49% GFP-positive Rollers (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, quantifying editing efficiency in the Roller cohort.

claim: GFP::CSR-1(+) Rollers increased from 8.8% (unmodified) to 28% (TEG) and 32.8% (RNA::TEG) in C. elegans.
source: Similarly, GFP::CSR-1(+) Rollers increased from 8.8% (unmodified) to 28% (TEG) and 32.8% (RNA::TEG) (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, quantifying editing efficiency at the csr-1 locus.

claim: TEG- and RNA::TEG-modified eft-3 and csr-1 donors produced >50% GFP(+) non-Roller progeny in C. elegans.
source: TEG- and RNA::TEG-modified eft-3 and csr-1 donors produced >50% GFP(+) non-Roller progeny compared to roughly 22% (eft-3) and 30% (csr-1) GFP(+) non-Rollers produced by the unmodified donors (Figure 4D and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and G, quantifying editing efficiency in the non-Roller cohort.

claim: Every GFP(+) C. elegans animal tested transmitted the edit to the next generation.
source: Every GFP(+) animal tested transmitted the edit to the next generation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by germline transmission data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: End-modified donors frequently yielded more than 100 independent GFP(+) F1 progeny from a single injected C. elegans hermaphrodite.
source: Strikingly, end-modified donors frequently yielded more than 100 independent GFP(+) F1 progeny from a single injected hermaphrodite.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from C. elegans germline editing experiments.

claim: The frequency of precise editing at the zebrafish Hey2 locus was 11-fold higher with the RNA::TEG donor (4.4%) than with the unmodified donor (0.4%).
source: Strikingly, the frequency of precise editing was 11-fold higher with the RNA::TEG (4.4%) donor than with the unmodified donor (0.4%) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-throughput sequencing data from zebrafish zygote injections shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The TEG-modified donor failed to enhance precise editing in zebrafish zygotes at the Hey2 locus.
source: The TEG-modified donor however failed to enhance precise editing in zebrafish zygotes (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-throughput sequencing data from zebrafish zygote injections shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The RNA::TEG-modified donor yielded more than twice as many pigmented F0 mice (37.9% uniform or mosaic) compared to unmodified donor (17.4%) at the Tyr locus.
source: The RNA::TEG-modified donor yielded more than twice as many pigmented F0 mice (37.9% uniform or mosaic) compared to unmodified donor (17.4%) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic analysis of founder mice shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 92% of the edited founders produced by the RNA::TEG-modified donor had uniformly pigmented coats, whereas only 62.5% of the edited F0 produced by the unmodified donor had uniformly pigmented coat color.
source: Strikingly, most (92%) of the edited founders produced by the RNA::TEG-modified donor had uniformly pigmented coats, whereas only 62.5% of the edited F0 produced by the unmodified donor had a uniformly pigmented coat color (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that the RNA::TEG-modified donor promotes editing during early zygotic divisions.
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, with inference about timing of editing.

claim: F0 mice with pigmented coat transmitted the corrected Tyrc-cor allele to F1 pups.
source: We confirmed that F0 mice with pigmented coat transmitted the corrected Tyrc-cor allele to F1 pups (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by germline transmission data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: The V5 tag was precisely inserted into the Sox2 locus in only 5.7% (n = 35) of F0 animals from injection with unmodified donor.
source: The V5 tag was precisely inserted into the Sox2 locus in only 5.7% (n = 35) of F0 animals from the injection with unmodified donor.
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data from mouse zygote injections targeting the Sox2 locus.

claim: The RNA::TEG-modified donor resulted in precise insertion of V5 in 33.3% (n = 24) of the F0 animals at the Sox2 locus—a greater than 5-fold increase in precise editing.
source: By contrast, the RNA::TEG-modified donor resulted in precise insertion of V5 in 33.3% (n = 24) of the F0 animals—a greater than 5-fold increase in precise editing (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: All of the V5-positive founders tested (one F0 from the unmodified donor and six F0s from RNA::TEG-modified donor) transmitted the Sox2::V5 allele to F1 progeny.
source: All of the V5-positive founders tested (one F0 from the unmodified donor and six F0s from RNA::TEG-modified donor) transmitted the Sox2::V5 allele to F1 progeny and the insertion was confirmed by Sanger sequencing (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by germline transmission data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B, C.

claim: Unmodified dsDNA formed concatemers within 1 hr after nucleofection into HEK293T cells.
source: We found that the unmodified dsDNA formed concatemers within 1 hr after nucleofection.
evidence: The claim is supported by Southern blot analysis of donor DNA over time after nucleofection.

claim: Concatemers of unmodified dsDNA composed of up to 10 copies were present within 3 hr after nucleofection and peaked in abundance by 12 hr.
source: Concatemers of up to 10 copies were present within 3 hr after nucleofection and peaked in abundance by 12 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by Southern blot analysis showing time-dependent concatemer formation.

claim: TEG-modified DNA showed a marked delay in the formation and levels of multimers compared to unmodified DNA.
source: By contrast, the TEG-modified DNA showed a marked delay in the formation and levels of multimers (Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 6B comparing modified and unmodified donors.

claim: TEG-modified DNA dimers and trimers gradually formed over the first 12–24 hr but were present at much lower levels than those formed by unmodified DNA.
source: Dimers and trimers gradually formed over the first 12–24 hr but were present at much lower levels than those formed by unmodified DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by Southern blot analysis comparing concatemer formation kinetics.

claim: At late time points (24, 48, and 72 hr after transfection), a greater fraction of TEG-modified DNA monomers than unmodified monomers was observed.
source: At late time points—24, 48, and 72 hr after transfection—we observed a greater fraction of TEG-modified DNA monomers than unmodified monomers (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The 5′-TEG modification suppresses concatemer formation.
source: These results suggest that the 5′-TEG modification suppresses concatemer formation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Southern blot data showing reduced concatemer formation with TEG-modified donors.

claim: TEG-modified DNA produced 19-fold fewer GUIDE-seq reads (genome wide) than unmodified DNA.
source: Strikingly, the TEG-modified DNA produced 19-fold fewer GUIDE-seq reads (genome wide) than did the unmodified DNA (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUIDE-seq analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The number of TEG-modified DNA insertions at the on-target ARHGEF9 locus and at the top 6 off-target sites was dramatically reduced, ranging from 15-fold to 6-fold lower compared to insertions of the unmodified DNA.
source: The number of TEG-modified DNA insertions obtained at the on-target cut site in the ARHGEF9 locus and at the top 6 off-target sites was dramatically reduced, ranging from 15-fold to 6-fold lower compared to insertions of the unmodified DNA (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUIDE-seq analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: TEG modifications suppress direct ligation of donor molecules both to each other and to chromosomal DSBs.
source: Taken together these data suggest that TEG modifications suppress direct ligation of donor molecules both to each other and to chromosomal DSBs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Southern blot and GUIDE-seq data showing reduced concatemerization and chromosomal integration.

claim: In mammalian cells, donors containing TEG or 2′OMe-RNA::TEG on their 5′-ends improved HDR efficacy.
source: In mammalian cells, donors containing simple modifications such as TEG or 2′OMe-RNA::TEG on their 5′-ends improved HDR efficacy.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from multiple mammalian cell experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: 5′-modifications increased the potency of ssDNA and dsDNA (long and short) donors, allowing efficient editing at significantly lower amounts.
source: These modifications increased the potency of ssDNA and dsDNA (long and short) donors, allowing efficient editing at significantly lower amounts.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from dose-response experiments with various donor types.

claim: Modifying the ends of the donors suppressed concatemer formation and reduced random integration of short dsDNA at chromosomal DSBs.
source: Modifying the ends of the donors suppressed concatemer formation and reduced random integration of short dsDNA at chromosomal DSBs.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from Southern blot and GUIDE-seq experiments.

claim: On long donors, end modification caused a ~2- to 5-fold increase in HDR frequency compared to unmodified donors without changing the donor concentration where efficacy reached its plateau.
source: On long donors end modification caused a ~2- to 5-fold increase in HDR frequency (total efficacy) compared to unmodified donors and did so without changing the donor concentration where efficacy reached its plateau.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from long donor experiments in mammalian cells.

claim: On short ssODN and dsDNA donors, end modifications exhibited increased potency but no increase in maximal efficacy.
source: In contrast, on short donors end modifications did not increase the maximal efficacy of HDR, but instead dramatically reduced the amount of donor required to reach that maximal level.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from short donor experiments in mammalian cells.

claim: The dose-limiting toxicity of ssODNs could be driven by total number of free DNA ends per cell, while longer molecules could encounter dose-limiting toxicity driven by total DNA mass.
source: For example, the dose-limiting toxicity of ssODNs could be driven by total number of free DNA ends per cell, while longer molecules could encounter dose-limiting toxicity driven by total DNA mass.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning to explain observed differences in how modifications affect long vs. short donors.

claim: Unmodified long dsDNA donors begin to plateau in efficacy at nearly 4-fold more mass, but ~10-fold lower molar amounts than ssODNs.
source: Consistent with this idea, unmodified long dsDNA donors begin to plateau in efficacy at nearly 4-fold more mass, but ~10-fold lower molar amounts than ssODNs.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of dose-response data from different donor types.

claim: RNA::TEG-modified donors significantly increased the levels of precision editing in C. elegans, zebrafish, and mice.
source: RNA::TEG-modified donors significantly increased the levels of precision editing in three different model organisms (C. elegans, zebrafish, and mice).
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from in vivo editing experiments in three animal models.

claim: High HDR efficiencies were achieved using end-modified dsDNA donors in C. elegans, zebrafish, and mice, which in some cases approached efficiencies previously observed for ssODN donors.
source: In all three animals, high HDR efficiencies were achieved using end-modified dsDNA donors, which in some cases approached efficiencies previously observed for ssODN donors (Dokshin et al., 2018; Kan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from animal editing experiments, with comparison to previously published ssODN results.

claim: Precise insertions were obtained with relatively short homology arms (less than 90 bp in mouse zygote injections).
source: Importantly, precise insertions were obtained with relatively short homology arms. For example, in mouse zygote injections, we used donors with homology arms of less than 90 bp, similar to typical arm lengths used for ssODN donors (Quadros et al., 2017) and at relatively low concentrations (1 ng/µl).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental design and results from mouse zygote injections, with citation to typical ssODN protocols.

claim: 5′-modifications help increase the efficacy of donors, in part, by suppressing non-homologous end-joining reactions.
source: Our findings suggest that they do so, in part, by suppressing non-homologous end-joining reactions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing reduced concatemerization and chromosomal integration.

claim: In several systems dsDNA donors have been shown to quickly form extrachromosomal arrays.
source: In several systems dsDNA donors have been shown to quickly form extrachromosomal arrays (Perucho et al., 1980; Folger et al., 1982; Mello et al., 1991) and may do so directly in the cytoplasm (Forbes et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous literature demonstrating extrachromosomal array formation.

claim: DNA delivered into the cytoplasm of the C. elegans gonadal syncytium gains entry into oocytes over a 24 hr period in a manner more consistent with cytoplasmic flow than with direct nuclear uptake by germ nuclei.
source: For example, DNA delivered into the cytoplasm of the C. elegans gonadal syncytium gains entry into oocytes over a 24 hr period in a manner more consistent with cytoplasmic flow than with direct nuclear uptake by germ nuclei (Ghanta and Mello, 2020), and transformants established in this way have been shown to contain concatenated arrays of injected DNA, several hundred kilobases in length, which then partition to progeny in a non-Mendelian fashion as extrachromosomal elements (Mello et al., 1991; Stinchcomb et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous work characterizing DNA delivery and array formation in C. elegans.

claim: Integration of extrachromosomal arrays into the host genome have been reported in zebrafish and mouse zygotes.
source: Integration of similar extrachromosomal arrays into the host genome have been reported in zebrafish and mouse zygotes (Stuart et al., 1988; Lacy et al., 1983; Costantini and Lacy, 1981).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous literature reporting array integration in vertebrate zygotes.

claim: The suppression of donor concatemer formation by 5′-modified donors could increase the effective molar amounts of donor available for precise repair of the target DSB.
source: Thus, the suppression of donor concatemer formation by 5′-modified donors could increase the effective molar amounts of donor available for precise repair of the target DSB.
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic inference based on experimental data showing reduced concatemerization.

claim: The suppression of direct ligation to chromosomal DNA through end-joining reactions could increase precision repair.
source: Similarly, once in the nucleus, the suppression of direct ligation to chromosomal DNA through end-joining reactions could further increase precision repair.
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic inference based on GUIDE-seq data showing reduced chromosomal integration.

claim: Modification of a single end was nearly as effective as modifications to both ends of the donor.
source: Perhaps consistent with suppression of concatenation as a major mechanism of action, it is intriguing that modification of a single end was nearly as effective as modifications to both ends of the donor.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data comparing single-end vs. double-end modifications, with mechanistic inference.

claim: A single end modification would limit concatenation to dimer formation.
source: In principle, a single end modification would limit concatenation to dimer formation.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference about the structural consequences of single-end modification.

claim: Modification of a single end could prevent donors from ligating into circles which might then concatenate further through HDR.
source: Similarly, modification of a single end could prevent donors from ligating into circles which might then concatenate further through HDR.
evidence: The claim is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the effectiveness of single-end modifications.

claim: A free unmodified 3′-end was required for efficient HDR.
source: We found that a free unmodified 3′-end was required for efficient HDR.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing that 3′-terminal modifications block HDR enhancement.

claim: By suppressing ligation, the 5′-modification maintains available 3′-ends, perhaps to prime repair synthesis.
source: Thus, by suppressing ligation, the 5′-modification in effect maintains available 3′-ends, perhaps to prime repair synthesis.
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic inference combining observations about 5′-modification effects and 3′-end requirements.

claim: In previous studies, fluorescent and amine modifications to the 5′- and 3′-termini of ssODN donors did not improve HDR efficacy over unmodified donors.
source: In previous studies, fluorescent and amine modifications to the 5′- and 3′-termini of ssODN donors did not improve HDR efficacy over unmodified donors (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to previous literature.

claim: PS linkages were shown to improve HDR in previous studies.
source: Similarly, PS linkages were shown to improve HDR (Renaud et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies with fluorescent/amine modifications and PS linkages were performed using much higher concentrations than the optimal concentrations for modified donors determined in this study.
source: However, these studies were performed using much higher concentrations than the optimal concentrations for modified donors determined here.
evidence: The claim compares experimental conditions between previous studies and the current work.

claim: ssODNs with PS linkages did not improve HDR at doses where RNA::TEG- and TEG-modified donors were most efficacious in this study.
source: In our study, ssODNs with PS linkages did not improve HDR at doses where RNA::TEG- and TEG-modified donors were most efficacious.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data comparing PS linkages to other modifications.

claim: One study showed that the addition of biotin improved HDR and favored single copy insertion in the rice fish medaka.
source: One study showed that the addition of biotin improved HDR and favored single copy insertion in the rice fish medaka (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to previous literature.

claim: The biotin moiety in the medaka study was attached to the donor via a polyethylene glycol (PEG) linker, but the study did not explore donors with PEG alone.
source: The biotin moiety was attached to the donor via a polyethylene glycol (PEG) linker, but the study did not explore donors with PEG alone.
evidence: The claim is based on citation and description of previous literature.

claim: Yu et al., 2020, showed that PEG10 with a 6-carbon linker boosted precise GFP insertions in vertebrate cells similar to those reported for TEG- and RNA::TEG-modified donors.

evidence: The claim is based on citation to previous work.

claim: Preliminary findings suggest that melting an 800 bp donor did not improve HDR efficiency in human cells.
source: Preliminary findings suggest that melting an 800 bp donor did not improve HDR efficiency in human cells (data not shown) but further studies are required to more rigorously test the impact of melting donors of greater length, and directed at more target sites, and of course to explore other physical perturbations.
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished preliminary data mentioned in the discussion.

claim: It is not known why donors modified with TEG and RNA::TEG performed similarly in C. elegans, while RNA::TEG was consistently superior to TEG alone in zebrafish and human cells.
source: We do not know why donors modified with TEG and RNA::TEG performed similarly in C. elegans, while RNA::TEG was consistently superior to TEG alone in zebrafish and human cells.
evidence: The claim acknowledges an unexplained observation from the experimental data.

claim: TEG alone may be sufficient to stabilize donor molecules for HDR in meiotic pachytene nuclei that are actively engaged in DNA recombination.
source: Perhaps TEG alone is sufficient to stabilize donor molecules for HDR in meiotic cells that are actively engaged in DNA recombination, while increased stability is required to enable donors to persist longer and thus to engage a much less active HDR repair machinery in mitotic cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning to explain observed differences between C. elegans and other systems.

claim: The RNA::TEG modification might facilitate editing in mitotic cells by providing improved protection from nuclease activity compared to TEG alone.
source: The RNA::TEG modification might therefore facilitate editing in mitotic cells by providing this measure of improved protection from nuclease activity compared to TEG alone.

claim: PS linkages are known to protect against nuclease activity.
source: PS linkages are known to protect against nuclease activity (Renaud et al., 2016), and it will therefore be interesting to explore whether a combination of internal (e.g., PS linkages) and terminal (e.g., 5′-RNA::TEG or 5′-TEG) modifications can further increase HDR efficacy.
evidence: The claim is based on citation to previous literature, with speculation about future experiments.

claim: Linear DNA molecules are known to form extensive homology-mediated and ligation-dependent concatemers upon delivery into animal cells or embryos.
source: Upon delivery into animal cells or embryos, linear DNA molecules are known to form extensive homology-mediated and ligation-dependent concatemers (Figure 6A; Perucho et al., 1980; Folger et al., 1982; Mello et al., 1991).

claim: High concentrations of dsDNA cause cytotoxicity in many cell types, limiting the number of long donor molecules that can be safely delivered into cells.
source: In many cell types, high concentrations of dsDNA cause cytotoxicity, limiting the number of long donor molecules that can be safely delivered into cells.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about dsDNA toxicity in cells.

claim: Long donor molecules may not transit the nuclear envelope as efficiently due to their size, reducing the effective concentration at the site of repair.
source: In addition, due to their size, long donor molecules may not transit the nuclear envelope as efficiently, reducing the effective concentration at the site of repair, or requiring cell division to gain access to the target locus.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about potential barriers to long donor efficacy.

claim: End-joining ligation reactions assemble linear dsDNA molecules into concatemers in eukaryotic cells.
source: Moreover, end-joining ligation reactions assemble linear dsDNA molecules into concatemers in eukaryotic cells (Perucho et al., 1980; Folger et al., 1982; Mello et al., 1991; Stuart et al., 1988; Lacy et al., 1983), further limiting the number of individual donor molecules and their ability to diffuse to their DSB target sites.
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous literature demonstrating concatemer formation.

claim: Concatemer formation limits the number of individual donor molecules and their ability to diffuse to their DSB target sites.
source: Moreover, end-joining ligation reactions assemble linear dsDNA molecules into concatemers in eukaryotic cells (Perucho et al., 1980; Folger et al., 1982; Mello et al., 1991; Stuart et al., 1988; Lacy et al., 1983), further limiting the number of individual donor molecules and their ability to diffuse to their DSB target sites.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the functional consequences of concatemer formation, based on cited literature.

claim: HDR is frequently less efficient when longer double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) templates are used as donors compared to short single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN) donors.
source: In many organisms and cell types, high HDR efficiencies are readily achieved using short single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN) donor templates that permit single base changes or short insertions or deletions. However, HDR is frequently less efficient when longer double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) templates are used as donors.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge and observations in the genome editing field.

claim: It is not known why longer DNA donors yield lower rates of HDR.
source: It is not known why longer DNA donors yield lower rates of HDR.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a gap in current understanding that motivates the study.

claim: Maximizing precision genome editing requires understanding how cells respond both to DSBs and to exogenous donors.
source: Maximizing precision genome editing, therefore, requires understanding how cells respond both to DSBs and to exogenous donors.
evidence: The claim is a logical statement about requirements for optimizing genome editing.

claim: Cell responses to DSBs and donors can be influenced by cell-intrinsic factors (e.g., genetics, cell type, and cell cycle stage) and cell-extrinsic factors (e.g., donor length, strandedness, and chemistry).
source: These responses can be influenced by many variables, including cell-intrinsic factors (e.g., genetics, cell type, and cell cycle stage) and cell-extrinsic factors (e.g., donor length, strandedness, and chemistry) (Lin et al., 2014; Wienert et al., 2020; Nambiar et al., 2019; Renaud et al., 2016; Rees et al., 2019; Jayathilaka et al., 2008; Pinder et al., 2015; Riesenberg and Maricic, 2018; Yu et al., 2015; Canny et al., 2018; Robert et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous literature documenting various factors affecting genome editing.

claim: Variables affecting cell responses can influence the relative efficiency of HDR compared to competing DSB repair pathways, such as non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).
source: Each of these variables can influence the relative efficiency of HDR compared to competing DSB repair pathways, such as non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) (Frank-Vaillant and Marcand, 2002; Mao et al., 2008; Chu et al., 2015; Maruyama et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous literature about DSB repair pathway competition.
